extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, and storytellers studying film/story design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on structural choices and storytelling principles for film screenplays, covering temporal design, causality, reality consistency, change vs stasis, politics of form, and setting dimensions. Useful for writers learning how to design stories that work for intended audiences and production constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear Versus Nonlinear Time
rubrics_metrics.description: A story told in LINEAR TIME begins at a point, moves elliptically through more or less continuous time, and ends later; flashbacks, if used, are handled so the audience can place the story's events in temporal order. A story told in NONLINEAR TIME skips helter-skelter through time or blurs temporal continuity so the audience cannot sort what happens before and after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using flashbacks ensure the audience can place events in temporal order. Antiplot devices toss time (e.g., BAD TIMING) to disconnect characters from the world and emphasize character-destiny. Use linear time for clarity and causality; use nonlinear time deliberately to produce fragmentation, subjective effect, or to express themes that require temporal distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality Versus Coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: CAUSALITY drives stories in which motivated actions cause effects that become causes of further effects, interlinking levels of conflict into a chain reaction toward the Story Climax. COINCIDENCE drives fictional worlds in which unmotivated actions trigger events that do not cause further effects, fragmenting the story into divergent episodes and often yielding an open ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose causality (Archplot) to express interconnectedness and meaningful cause-effect chains; choose coincidence (Antiplot) to emphasize randomness, absurdity, or disconnectedness (example: AFTER HOURS shows a character buffeted by random collisions). Be aware that coincidence-based design tends to produce fragmentation and may reduce audience expectation of closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent Versus Inconsistent Realities
rubrics_metrics.description: CONSISTENT REALITIES are fictional settings that establish modes of interaction between characters and their world and keep those rules consistent throughout the telling. INCONSISTENT REALITIES mix modes of interaction so episodes jump from one 'reality' to another to create absurdity; antiplot often breaks previously established rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you create story rules (even bizarre ones), you must work within them; breaking them arbitrarily undermines coherence. Consistent reality sustains audience belief (e.g., fantasy that follows its whimsical laws). Inconsistent reality can work when it coheres to a subjective perception or filmmaker's private world (e.g., WEEKEND), but expect a smaller, more adventurous audience and ensure the inconsistency serves a unifying subjective effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change Versus Stasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories above the line (toward Miniplot and Archplot) are those in which life clearly changes; stories below the line remain in STASIS and do not arc, dissolving into portraiture rather than telling a classical story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'change' (Archplot/Miniplot) when you want an arc and irreversible transformation for the protagonist. Use 'stasis' (Nonplot) for portraiture, slice-of-life, or absurdist cycles where the character's condition at the end is virtually identical to the opening. Recognize Nonplot informs or moves the audience inward but does not fit the classical story triangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics of Story Design (Hollywood vs Art Film)
rubrics_metrics.description: The political/cultural split between 'Hollywood film' and 'art film' reflects different worldviews: Hollywood tends to optimistic belief in change, reliance on Archplot and positive endings; art film tends toward pessimism, Miniplot/Antiplot/Nonplot, and negative or ambiguous endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how your political and commercial choices affect audience size, budget, and distribution. Hollywood-oriented Archplot films have larger audiences and budgets; art-film choices often imply lower budgets and niche audiences. Be honest about where you 'reside' on the story triangle and make pragmatic decisions—if you want commercial reach, lean toward Archplot; if you accept small audiences and low budgets, Miniplot/Antiplot may be viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Writer Must Earn His Living Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: As story design moves away from the Archplot toward Miniplot, Antiplot, and Nonplot, the audience shrinks, which in turn forces lower budgets and fewer commercial opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you plan to write minimalism or antistructure, find non-Hollywood producers and accept lower pay and smaller budgets. If you want mainstream (Hollywood) opportunities, be aware that studios expect scripts that can reach large audiences—typically stories that lean toward the Archplot.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Writer Must Master Classical Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Miniplot and Antiplot are reactions to the Classical (Archplot); serious writers first master the classical Archplot form before effectively shrinking or subverting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and practice Archplot until the form becomes craft, then play with or against it. Examples: Bergman, Fellini, Godard, Altman, and Hitchcock worked within classical forms before experimenting. To successfully create Miniplot/Antiplot you must understand what you are reversing; naive imitation of avant-garde techniques without mastery yields pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play With or Against Classical Expectancy When Using Miniplot/Antiplot
rubrics_metrics.description: Because audiences enter stories with Classical anticipation, to make Miniplot and Antiplot work the writer must carefully and creatively shatter or bend that expectancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate subversion of classical expectations can guide the audience into accepting internalized passivity or absurdity, but it must be done with craft. Randomly avoiding closure, activity, chronology, and causality for ideological reasons often results in pretense rather than artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Writer Must Believe in What He Writes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tale you create proclaims to the audience: 'I believe life is like this.' The writer must have passionate conviction in the form and meaning they choose—otherwise the work smells phony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask yourself why your screenplay falls into a corner of the triangle. If you don't genuinely believe in minimalism/anticlassicism, do not adopt those forms for political or stylistic posturing. Authenticity of belief is essential; writing 'what you're not' produces insincere, derivative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: The War on Cliche / Knowledge of the Story World
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliche stems from the writer's lack of intimate knowledge of the fictional world; writers who don't know their setting crib scenes, dialogue, and characters from existing works, producing reheated, boring material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality and excellence require in-depth understanding and insight into the world of your story. Research and immerse yourself in the setting (period, locale, culture, practices) to avoid leaning on secondhand tropes and to win the 'war on cliche.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Period
rubrics_metrics.description: PERIOD is a story's place in time: contemporary, historical, hypothetical future, or timeless fantasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and make clear the story's temporal period; this shapes costumes, language, cultural references, and the story's thematic possibilities. Some works intentionally obscure period (e.g., ANIMAL FARM) — do so only if it serves theme and internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: DURATION is a story's length through time: how much time the story spans in the lives of characters (decades, years, months, days). Screentime can equal, exceed, or be less than storytime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate duration for the story you want to tell. Techniques (cross-cutting, overlap, repetition, slow motion) can expand screentime beyond storytime (example: 'Odessa Steps' sequence). Rare works may equate storytime and screentime (e.g., MY DINNER WITH ANDRE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Location
rubrics_metrics.description: LOCATION is the story's physical dimension: the specific geography, town, streets, buildings, rooms, landscape or even planet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about where the story takes place; granular physical detail grounds the narrative and enables original, non-clichéd scenes. Consider the precise spaces characters inhabit and how those spaces shape action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Level of Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: LEVEL OF CONFLICT is the fourth dimension of setting (along with Period, Duration, Location) that defines the intensity and scope of struggle in the story world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not fully expanded in this section, identify whether conflict is intimate or epic, individual or societal; the level of conflict interacts with period, duration, and location to determine genre tone and audience expectations.
